# This session

- a table with **nineteen** columns, and what plain regression does with it
- a **penalty** on the size of the coefficients: ridge regression
- why the penalty needs every column on the same **scale**, and a pipeline
- choosing the penalty's strength with the folds: **hyperparameter tuning**
- the **lasso**, which sets coefficients to exactly zero, and the elastic net
- what the arguments of these scikit-learn objects do, and when to change them

Part 1
:::

A wider table, and what ordinary least squares does with it.

# The question

**How volatile will the whole market be over the next twenty trading days?**

::: {.why-grid}
::: {.why-point}
**Why it matters** <span>the risk of almost any portfolio moves with the index, so its volatility sets margins, limits and option prices</span>
:::
::: {.why-point}
**What you know today** <span>the index's own history over several windows, and how volatile each stock in it has been lately</span>
:::
:::

# Splitting by date

```{pyodide}
train = table.loc[:"2022-12-31"]
test = table.loc["2023-01-01":]

columns = list(table.columns[:-1])
print(len(train), len(test), len(columns))
```

`table.columns[:-1]` is every column except the last, which is the target.


# A helper for the error

```{pyodide}
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error

def rmse(actual, predicted):
    return np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(actual, predicted))
```

The RMSE is computed many times this session. A two-line function keeps every
later cell short.


# One column, as before

```{pyodide}
one = LinearRegression()
one.fit(train[["vol_20d"]], train["vol_next"])

print("train:", rmse(train["vol_next"], one.predict(train[["vol_20d"]])))
print("test :", rmse(test["vol_next"], one.predict(test[["vol_20d"]])))
```

This is the same model as last time, on the index. A test error of 0.237 is
the number to beat.


# All nineteen columns

```{pyodide}
ols = LinearRegression()
ols.fit(train[columns], train["vol_next"])

print("train:", rmse(train["vol_next"], ols.predict(train[columns])))
print("test :", rmse(test["vol_next"], ols.predict(test[columns])))
```

The training error fell and the test error rose. Eighteen extra columns made
the forecast worse.


# The nineteen coefficients

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
_ols = LinearRegression().fit(TRAIN[COLS], TRAIN["vol_next"])
_b = pd.Series(_ols.coef_, index=COLS)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10.6, 4.3))
ax.barh(range(len(_b)), _b.values, color=[BLUE if v >= 0 else BRICK for v in _b.values],
        height=0.62)
ax.set_yticks(range(len(_b)))
ax.set_yticklabels(_b.index, fontsize=9.5)
ax.invert_yaxis()
ax.axvline(0, color=GREY, linewidth=1)
ax.set_xlabel("coefficient (ordinary least squares)")
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
for i, v in enumerate(_b.values):
    ax.text(v + (0.012 if v >= 0 else -0.012), i, "%.2f" % v, va="center",
            ha="left" if v >= 0 else "right", fontsize=9, color="#52514e")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Higher volatility at J&J and JPMorgan **lowers** the forecast, and the index's
own volatility raises it at 60 days and lowers it at 120. Those signs are not
believable.


# The columns are near-copies of each other

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
_c = TRAIN[COLS].corr()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 4.35))
im = ax.imshow(_c.values, cmap="Blues", vmin=-0.2, vmax=1)
ax.set_xticks(range(len(COLS)))
ax.set_yticks(range(len(COLS)))
ax.set_xticklabels(COLS, rotation=90, fontsize=8)
ax.set_yticklabels(COLS, fontsize=8)
ax.grid(False)
cb = fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=0.045, pad=0.03)
cb.ax.tick_params(labelsize=8.5)
cb.set_label("correlation", fontsize=9.5)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

`vol_40d` and `vol_60d` correlate at 0.93. Two columns with the same
information can take +5 and −4.8 and fit exactly as well as +0.1 and +0.1.
The fit is fine; the coefficients are noise.


# The coefficients depend on the rows

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
_show = ["vol_60d", "vol_120d", "JNJ_vol", "XOM_vol"]
_ols_f, _rdg_f = [], []
for _fi, _sc in FOLDS.split(TRAIN):
    _blk = TRAIN.iloc[_fi]
    _ols_f.append(LinearRegression().fit(_blk[COLS], _blk["vol_next"]).coef_)
    _rdg_f.append(Ridge(alpha=1000).fit(_blk[COLS], _blk["vol_next"]).coef_)
_ols_f = np.array(_ols_f)
_rdg_f = np.array(_rdg_f)
_idx = [COLS.index(s) for s in _show]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10.6, 3.0))
for k in range(5):
    ax.scatter(np.arange(4) + (k - 2) * 0.07, _ols_f[k, _idx], s=46, color=BLUE,
               zorder=3)
ax.axhline(0, color=GREY, linewidth=1)
ax.set_xticks(range(4))
ax.set_xticklabels(_show)
ax.set_ylabel("coefficient")
ax.set_title("Ordinary least squares, fitted on each of the five fold blocks", loc="left")
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Each column has five dots, one per block of training rows. `vol_120d` is +1.02
on one block and −0.94 on another. A coefficient that changes sign with the sample
cannot be used for next year.

::: {.diagram}

:::

::: {.keypoint}
Subset selection asks, for each column, in or out. A penalty asks a softer
question: **how large may its coefficient be?**
:::


# 2 · Ridge regression {.divider}

::: {.divider-kicker}
Part 2
:::

::: {.divider-note}
A penalty on the squared coefficients, and one new argument.
:::


# What ordinary least squares minimises

::: {.formula}
$$
\text{RSS} = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(y_i - \hat{y}_i\right)^2
$$
:::

The residual sum of squares on the training rows, and nothing else. A
coefficient of +5 is accepted if it lowers the RSS by a little, which is how
+5 and −4.8 on two near-copies come about.


# The ridge objective

::: {.formula}
$$
\text{RSS} + \alpha \sum_{j=1}^{p} \beta_j^2
$$
:::

Ridge adds a charge for the size of the slopes. A coefficient of 5 now costs
25 times `alpha`, and is kept only if it lowers the RSS by more than that.

::: {.muted .small}
The sum runs over the slopes and leaves the intercept alone.
:::


# What alpha does

::: {.diagram}
<svg width="1000" height="200" viewBox="0 0 1000 200" role="img" aria-label="A line from alpha equals zero, which is ordinary least squares, to alpha very large, where every coefficient is zero">
  <line x1="130" y1="90" x2="870" y2="90" stroke="#c3c2b7" stroke-width="4"/>
  <circle cx="130" cy="90" r="14" fill="#1c5cab"/>
  <circle cx="500" cy="90" r="14" fill="#d99a1c"/>
  <circle cx="870" cy="90" r="14" fill="#b3402f"/>
  <g font-family="Segoe UI, sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">
    <text x="130" y="46" font-size="22" fill="#0d366b" font-weight="600">alpha = 0</text>
    <text x="500" y="46" font-size="22" fill="#8a6508" font-weight="600">alpha in between</text>
    <text x="870" y="46" font-size="22" fill="#b3402f" font-weight="600">alpha very large</text>
    <text x="130" y="136" font-size="16" fill="#52514e">no penalty at all</text>
    <text x="130" y="160" font-size="16" fill="#52514e">ordinary least squares</text>
    <text x="500" y="136" font-size="16" fill="#52514e">every slope pulled towards zero</text>
    <text x="500" y="160" font-size="16" fill="#52514e">but none reaches it</text>
    <text x="870" y="136" font-size="16" fill="#52514e">every slope is zero</text>
    <text x="870" y="160" font-size="16" fill="#52514e">the forecast is the training average</text>
  </g>
</svg>
:::

::: {.keypoint}
`alpha` is the price of coefficient size. It is set before `.fit()` runs, and
the rows cannot choose it, because every value gives a fitted model.
:::


# Ridge in code

```{pyodide}
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge

ridge = Ridge(alpha=1000)
ridge.fit(train[columns], train["vol_next"])

print(rmse(test["vol_next"], ridge.predict(test[columns])))
```

Only the first line changed: `Ridge` fits and predicts exactly like
`LinearRegression`. 0.228, against 0.248 unpenalised and 0.237 for one column.

#| autorun: false

small.fit(train[columns], train["vol_next"])
print("alpha small:", rmse(test["vol_next"], small.predict(test[columns])))

:::


# Your turn 1: answer

```python
small = Ridge(alpha=1)         # 0.247
large = Ridge(alpha=100000)    # 0.282
```

`alpha=1` is ordinary least squares to three decimals: a penalty of 1 is
nothing next to an RSS over 1,894 rows. `alpha=100000` is worse than repeating
this month, and at ten million the error is 0.291, the same as guessing the
average.

::: {.keypoint}
Too little penalty leaves the overfitting in. Too much removes the signal with
the noise.
:::


# Why smaller coefficients forecast better

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.6, 3.0), sharey=True)
for ax, arr, ttl, col in [(axes[0], _ols_f, "ordinary least squares", BLUE),
                          (axes[1], _rdg_f, "ridge, alpha = 1000", AMBER)]:
    for k in range(5):
        ax.scatter(np.arange(4) + (k - 2) * 0.07, arr[k, _idx], s=46, color=col,
                   zorder=3)
    ax.axhline(0, color=GREY, linewidth=1)
    ax.set_xticks(range(4))
    ax.set_xticklabels(_show)
    ax.set_title(ttl, loc="left")
    ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
axes[0].set_ylabel("coefficient, one dot per fold block")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

These are the same four columns on the same five blocks. The ridge coefficients
are small and they stay put, so a coefficient fitted on the past holds on the
years to come. That is a little bias in exchange for far less variance.


# 3 · The penalty and the units {.divider}

::: {.divider-kicker}
Part 3
:::

::: {.divider-note}
The penalty charges by coefficient size, and size depends on units.
:::


# The same column, in two units

::: {.diagram}
<svg width="1000" height="230" viewBox="0 0 1000 230" role="img" aria-label="The vol_20d column in percent and in decimals: the values, the coefficient OLS gives it, and the penalty ridge would charge">

  </g>

  <text x="660" y="90" text-anchor="middle" font-size="19" font-family="Cascadia Mono, monospace" fill="#0d366b" font-weight="600">0.019</text>
  <text x="870" y="90" text-anchor="middle" font-size="19" font-family="Cascadia Mono, monospace" fill="#0d366b" font-weight="600">0.0004</text>
  <rect x="20" y="130" width="960" height="62" rx="8" fill="#fbf1f0" stroke="#e0b3ac" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <text x="40" y="168" font-size="16" font-family="Cascadia Mono, monospace" fill="#b3402f">vol_20d in decimals</text>
  <text x="420" y="168" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" font-family="Cascadia Mono, monospace" fill="#26333f">0.0098  0.0121  0.0090</text>
  <text x="660" y="168" text-anchor="middle" font-size="19" font-family="Cascadia Mono, monospace" fill="#b3402f" font-weight="600">1.913</text>
  <text x="870" y="168" text-anchor="middle" font-size="19" font-family="Cascadia Mono, monospace" fill="#b3402f" font-weight="600">3.66</text>
  <text x="500" y="222" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-family="Segoe UI, sans-serif" fill="#52514e">the same column, the same forecast, and a penalty ten thousand times larger</text>
</svg>
:::

::: {.keypoint}
Ridge shrinks the column in small units first, whatever it contains. The
penalty is judging columns by their units, not by their usefulness.
:::


# Measured: OLS

```{pyodide}
train_dec = train.copy()
test_dec = test.copy()
train_dec["vol_20d"] = train_dec["vol_20d"] / 100
test_dec["vol_20d"] = test_dec["vol_20d"] / 100

spot = columns.index("vol_20d")

ols_dec = LinearRegression()
ols_dec.fit(train_dec[columns], train_dec["vol_next"])
print(ols.coef_[spot], ols_dec.coef_[spot])
print(rmse(test["vol_next"], ols.predict(test[columns])), rmse(test["vol_next"], ols_dec.predict(test_dec[columns])))
```

The coefficient is exactly one hundred times larger and the test error is
exactly the same.


# Measured: ridge

```{pyodide}
ridge_dec = Ridge(alpha=1000)
ridge_dec.fit(train_dec[columns], train_dec["vol_next"])

print(ridge.coef_[spot], ridge_dec.coef_[spot])
```

The coefficient on `vol_20d` falls from 0.031 to 0.0003. Ridge has dropped the
column, and nothing about its information changed.


# Put every column on the same scale

::: {.formula}
$$
z = \frac{x - \bar{x}}{s}
$$
:::

Subtract each column's mean and divide by its standard deviation. Every column
then has mean 0 and standard deviation 1, whatever units it arrived in, and one
coefficient is comparable with another.

::: {.muted .small}
The standardising formula from two sessions ago, where it was noted that
penalised regression needs it.
:::


# StandardScaler

```{pyodide}
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

scaler = StandardScaler()
scaler.fit(train[columns])
X_train = scaler.transform(train[columns])
X_test = scaler.transform(test[columns])

print(scaler.mean_[spot], scaler.scale_[spot])
print(round(X_train[:, spot].mean(), 6), round(X_train[:, spot].std(), 6))
```

`.fit()` learns each column's mean and standard deviation from the training
rows. `.transform()` applies them, to the test rows as well: their own mean is
information from the future.


# Ridge on standardised columns

```{pyodide}
ridge = Ridge(alpha=1000)
ridge.fit(X_train, train["vol_next"])

print(rmse(test["vol_next"], ridge.predict(X_test)))
```

With every column in standard deviations, the same model and the same alpha
score 0.218, down from 0.228.


# Reading standardised coefficients

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
_sc = StandardScaler().fit(TRAIN[COLS])
_rs = Ridge(alpha=1000).fit(_sc.transform(TRAIN[COLS]), TRAIN["vol_next"])
_bs = pd.Series(_rs.coef_, index=COLS).sort_values(ascending=False)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10.6, 4.0))
ax.bar(range(len(_bs)), _bs.values, color=[BLUE if v >= 0 else BRICK for v in _bs.values],
       width=0.62)
ax.set_xticks(range(len(_bs)))
ax.set_xticklabels(_bs.index, rotation=60, ha="right", fontsize=9.5)
ax.axhline(0, color=GREY, linewidth=1)
ax.set_ylabel("coefficient per standard deviation")
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The bars are comparable now. The last five and ten days matter most, a market
that fell in the last week is more volatile in the month after, and the other
stocks each add a little.


# Two steps that belong together

::: {.diagram}

The training rows are scaled and then fitted; the test rows are scaled the same
way and then predicted. Cross-validation repeats the pair on five fitting
blocks, so the scaler has to be refitted inside every fold with the model.


# Pipeline

```{pyodide}
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline

pipe = Pipeline([("scale", StandardScaler()), ("ridge", Ridge(alpha=1000))])
pipe.fit(train[columns], train["vol_next"])

print(rmse(test["vol_next"], pipe.predict(test[columns])))
```

A pipeline is a list of named steps. `.fit()` fits the scaler, transforms,
and fits the ridge; `.predict()` transforms with the fitted scaler and
predicts. The names are yours to choose.


# A pipeline is a model

```{pyodide}
from sklearn.model_selection import TimeSeriesSplit, cross_val_score

folds = TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=5)

scores = cross_val_score(pipe, train[columns], train["vol_next"],
                         cv=folds, scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error")
print(-scores.round(3))
print(-scores.mean())
```

`cross_val_score` takes the pipeline where it took `LinearRegression()` last
time, and refits the scaler inside each fold. The third fold still contains
March 2020.


# 4 · Choosing alpha {.divider}

::: {.divider-kicker}
Part 4
:::

::: {.divider-note}
A setting the data cannot pick, and the tool that searches over it.
:::


# Parameters and hyperparameters

<div class="compare">
<div class="compare-col">
<h3>Parameters</h3>
<p>The intercept and the nineteen slopes. <code>.fit()</code> computes them from the training rows and stores them with a trailing underscore.</p>
</div>
<div class="compare-col cmp-alt">
<h3>Hyperparameters</h3>
<p><code>alpha</code>. Passed in before <code>.fit()</code> and never changed by it. Every value gives a fitted model, so the training rows cannot say which value is right.</p>
</div>
</div>

::: {.keypoint}
A hyperparameter is chosen the way candidates were chosen last time: fit with
each value, score on held-out rows, keep the best.
:::


# Try several

```{pyodide}
for alpha in [1, 10, 100, 1000, 10000]:
    pipe = Pipeline([("scale", StandardScaler()), ("ridge", Ridge(alpha=alpha))])
    scores = cross_val_score(pipe, train[columns], train["vol_next"],
                             cv=folds, scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error")
    print(alpha, round(-scores.mean(), 4))
```

The cross-validated error falls to 1000 and rises again. The folds locate the
point between too little penalty and too much.


# The validation curve

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
_grid = np.logspace(0, 5, 26)
_cv = []
for _a in _grid:
    _p = Pipeline([("scale", StandardScaler()), ("ridge", Ridge(alpha=_a))])
    _cv.append(-cross_val_score(_p, TRAIN[COLS], TRAIN["vol_next"], cv=FOLDS,
                                scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error").mean())
_cv = np.array(_cv)
_best = int(np.argmin(_cv))
_ticks = [1, 10, 100, 1000, 10000, 100000]
_labels = ["1", "10", "100", "1,000", "10,000", "100,000"]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10.0, 3.1))
ax.plot(_grid, _cv, color=BLUE, linewidth=2.2)
ax.scatter([_grid[_best]], [_cv[_best]], s=90, color=AMBER, zorder=3)
ax.text(_grid[_best], _cv[_best] + 0.018, "lowest at alpha ≈ 1,600", ha="center",
        fontsize=11, color="#8a6508", fontweight="600")
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_xticks(_ticks)
ax.set_xticklabels(_labels)
ax.set_ylim(0.53, 0.74)
ax.set_xlabel("alpha")
ax.set_ylabel("cross-validated RMSE")
ax.text(2.2, 0.66, "too little penalty:\noverfitting", fontsize=11, color="#52514e")
ax.text(1.4e4, 0.565, "too much penalty:\nunderfitting", fontsize=11, color="#52514e")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

This is the same loop over a finer grid. High on the left where the penalty is too
weak, high on the right where it is too strong, lowest at a few thousand.


# Why the grid goes in factors of ten

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
_alphas = np.logspace(-1, 6, 60)
_Xs = _sc.transform(TRAIN[COLS])
_paths = np.array([Ridge(alpha=a).fit(_Xs, TRAIN["vol_next"]).coef_ for a in _alphas])
_hl = {"vol_5d": BLUE, "vol_10d": BLUE_LIGHT, "ret_5d": BRICK, "AAPL_vol": AMBER}
_rticks = [0.1, 1, 10, 100, 1000, 10000, 100000, 1000000]
_rlabels = ["0.1", "1", "10", "100", "1,000", "10,000", "100,000", "1,000,000"]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10.0, 3.1))
for j, name in enumerate(COLS):
    if name in _hl:
        ax.plot(_alphas, _paths[:, j], color=_hl[name], linewidth=2.0, label=name)
    else:
        ax.plot(_alphas, _paths[:, j], color=GREY_LIGHT, linewidth=1.0)
ax.axhline(0, color=GREY, linewidth=1)
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_xlim(0.08, 1.5e6)
ax.set_xticks(_rticks)
ax.set_xticklabels(_rlabels)
ax.set_xlabel("alpha")
ax.set_ylabel("coefficient")
ax.legend(loc="upper right", ncol=2)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Each line is one coefficient as alpha grows. Between 1 and 10 almost nothing
happens; between 1,000 and 10,000 everything does. The grid steps by a factor,
not by a fixed amount.

::: {.muted .small}
Five values times five folds is twenty-five fits, run by one call.
:::


# GridSearchCV in code

```{pyodide}
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV

pipe = Pipeline([("scale", StandardScaler()), ("ridge", Ridge())])
grid = {"ridge__alpha": [1, 10, 100, 1000, 10000]}

search = GridSearchCV(pipe, grid, cv=folds, scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error")
search.fit(train[columns], train["vol_next"])

print(search.best_params_)
print(-search.best_score_)
```

The grid is a dictionary of settings and the values to try. `"ridge__alpha"`
is the step name, two underscores, then the argument: that is how a setting
inside a pipeline is addressed.


# What the search holds afterwards

```{pyodide}
results = pd.DataFrame(search.cv_results_)
results[["param_ridge__alpha", "mean_test_score", "std_test_score", "rank_test_score"]]
```

`cv_results_` is the whole grid as a table: every value tried, its mean score
over the folds, the spread, and its rank.


# Predicting with the search

```{pyodide}
print(search.best_estimator_)
print(rmse(test["vol_next"], search.predict(test[columns])))
```

`best_estimator_` is the winning pipeline refitted on every training row, and
`search.predict()` uses it. The test rows are opened once, here, and played no
part in choosing alpha.


# The arguments of GridSearchCV

| argument | what it changes | when to change it |
|---|---|---|
| `estimator` | the model or pipeline being tuned | always a pipeline when scaling is involved |
| `param_grid` | the settings and the values to try | keep each list short; several keys multiply |
| `cv` | how the folds are made | always set it: the default ignores time order |
| `scoring` | the score, larger is better | match it to the error you will report |
| `refit` | refit the best on all training rows | leave `True`, so `.predict()` works |
| `n_jobs` | how many folds run at once | `-1` on your own machine, to use every core |
| `return_train_score` | also record the training score | to see how large the overfitting gap is |

: {.vocab}

# 5 · Lasso {.divider}

::: {.divider-kicker}
Part 5
:::

::: {.divider-note}
A different penalty, which sets coefficients to exactly zero.
:::


# One change to the penalty

::: {.formula}
$$
\text{ridge:}\quad \text{RSS} + \alpha \sum_{j=1}^{p} \beta_j^2
$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.formula}
$$
\text{lasso:}\quad \text{RSS} + \alpha \sum_{j=1}^{p} |\beta_j|
$$
:::

The squares become absolute values. Everything else is the same: a price on
size, set by alpha, chosen by cross-validation.
:::


# Why absolute values give exact zeros

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
_two = ["vol_10d", "vol_60d"]
_s2 = StandardScaler().fit(TRAIN[_two])
_X2 = _s2.transform(TRAIN[_two])
_y2 = TRAIN["vol_next"].values - TRAIN["vol_next"].mean()
_b_ols = LinearRegression(fit_intercept=False).fit(_X2, _y2).coef_
_b_rdg = Ridge(alpha=1000, fit_intercept=False).fit(_X2, _y2).coef_
_b_las = Lasso(alpha=0.1, fit_intercept=False).fit(_X2, _y2).coef_
_g1, _g2 = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(-0.35, 0.55, 160), np.linspace(-0.35, 0.4, 160))
_rss = np.zeros_like(_g1)
for _i in range(_g1.shape[0]):
    for _j in range(_g1.shape[1]):
        _res = _y2 - _X2 @ np.array([_g1[_i, _j], _g2[_i, _j]])
        _rss[_i, _j] = (_res ** 2).sum()
_rss0 = ((_y2 - _X2 @ _b_ols) ** 2).sum()
_levels = _rss0 * np.array([1.002, 1.01, 1.03, 1.07, 1.13, 1.22])

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.0, 3.7))
for ax, ttl, bpen, shape in [(axes[0], "ridge: the penalty region is a circle", _b_rdg, "circle"),
                             (axes[1], "lasso: the penalty region is a diamond", _b_las, "diamond")]:
    ax.contour(_g1, _g2, _rss, levels=_levels, colors=[GREY], linewidths=1.0)
    ax.axhline(0, color=GREY_LIGHT, linewidth=1)
    ax.axvline(0, color=GREY_LIGHT, linewidth=1)
    if shape == "circle":
        _rad = np.sqrt((bpen ** 2).sum())
        _th = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 200)
        ax.fill(_rad * np.cos(_th), _rad * np.sin(_th), color=BLUE_LIGHT, alpha=0.35)
        ax.plot(_rad * np.cos(_th), _rad * np.sin(_th), color=BLUE, linewidth=1.6)
    else:
        _t = np.abs(bpen).sum()
        ax.fill([_t, 0, -_t, 0], [0, _t, 0, -_t], color=BLUE_LIGHT, alpha=0.35)
        ax.plot([_t, 0, -_t, 0, _t], [0, _t, 0, -_t, 0], color=BLUE, linewidth=1.6)
    ax.scatter([_b_ols[0]], [_b_ols[1]], s=60, color=INK, zorder=4)
    ax.text(_b_ols[0] + 0.02, _b_ols[1] + 0.02, "OLS", fontsize=10.5, color=INK)
    ax.scatter([bpen[0]], [bpen[1]], s=80, color=AMBER, zorder=5)
    ax.text(bpen[0] - 0.03, bpen[1] - 0.07, "penalised", fontsize=10.5,
            color="#8a6508", fontweight="600", ha="right")
    ax.set_xlim(-0.35, 0.55)
    ax.set_ylim(-0.35, 0.4)
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.set_xlabel("coefficient on vol_10d")
    ax.set_title(ttl, loc="left", fontsize=12)
    ax.grid(False)
axes[0].set_ylabel("coefficient on vol_60d")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

With two columns the fit can be drawn. The grey rings are equal RSS around the OLS
point, and the penalised fit is the point of the shaded region on the smallest
ring it reaches. A diamond has corners on the axes, so the ring usually meets it
where one coefficient is exactly zero.


# The two paths

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
_la = np.logspace(-3.5, -0.3, 60)
_lpaths = np.array([Lasso(alpha=a, max_iter=20000).fit(_Xs, TRAIN["vol_next"]).coef_ for a in _la])
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.6, 3.1))
for ax, xs, ps, ttl in [(axes[0], _alphas, _paths, "ridge"),
                        (axes[1], _la, _lpaths, "lasso")]:
    for j, name in enumerate(COLS):
        if name in _hl:
            ax.plot(xs, ps[:, j], color=_hl[name], linewidth=2.0, label=name)
        else:
            ax.plot(xs, ps[:, j], color=GREY_LIGHT, linewidth=1.0)
    ax.axhline(0, color=GREY, linewidth=1)
    ax.set_xscale("log")
    ax.set_xlabel("alpha")
    ax.set_title(ttl, loc="left")
axes[0].set_xlim(0.08, 1.5e6)
axes[0].set_xticks([0.1, 10, 1000, 100000])
axes[0].set_xticklabels(["0.1", "10", "1,000", "100,000"])
axes[1].set_xlim(0.0003, 0.6)
axes[1].set_xticks([0.001, 0.01, 0.1])
axes[1].set_xticklabels(["0.001", "0.01", "0.1"])
axes[0].set_ylabel("coefficient")
axes[0].legend(loc="upper right", ncol=2, fontsize=9.5)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Ridge shrinks every coefficient smoothly and none reaches zero. Lasso drives
them to zero one at a time. The alpha scales differ too: ridge's useful range is
in the thousands here, lasso's is between 0.01 and 1.


# Lasso in code

```{pyodide}
from sklearn.linear_model import Lasso

lasso = Pipeline([("scale", StandardScaler()), ("lasso", Lasso(alpha=0.1))])
lasso.fit(train[columns], train["vol_next"])

print(rmse(test["vol_next"], lasso.predict(test[columns])))
```

The same pipeline with `Lasso` in the second step scores 0.217, level with
ridge.


# Which columns survived

```{pyodide}
coefs = lasso.named_steps["lasso"].coef_

for name, b in zip(columns, coefs):
    if b != 0:
        print(name, round(b, 3))
```

Fourteen of the nineteen coefficients are exactly zero. `named_steps["lasso"]`
reaches the fitted `Lasso` inside the pipeline, which has no `coef_` of its own.


# Choosing lasso's alpha

```{pyodide}
lasso_grid = {"lasso__alpha": [0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1]}

lasso_search = GridSearchCV(lasso, lasso_grid, cv=folds, scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error")
lasso_search.fit(train[columns], train["vol_next"])

print(lasso_search.best_params_)
print(-lasso_search.best_score_)
```

This is the same search with a grid on lasso's scale. Alpha 0.1 has the lowest
cross-validated error, 0.580 against 0.560 for ridge.


# The zeros are not a verdict

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
_keep = np.zeros((5, len(COLS)), dtype=bool)
for _k, (_fi, _sc_) in enumerate(FOLDS.split(TRAIN)):
    _blk = TRAIN.iloc[_fi]
    _m = Pipeline([("scale", StandardScaler()), ("lasso", Lasso(alpha=0.1, max_iter=20000))])
    _m.fit(_blk[COLS], _blk["vol_next"])
    _keep[_k] = _m.named_steps["lasso"].coef_ != 0
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10.6, 2.7))
for _k in range(5):
    for j in range(len(COLS)):
        ax.scatter([j], [4 - _k], s=110, marker="s",
                   color=BLUE if _keep[_k, j] else "#eeede7", zorder=3)
ax.set_xticks(range(len(COLS)))
ax.set_xticklabels(COLS, rotation=60, ha="right", fontsize=9)
ax.set_yticks(range(5))
ax.set_yticklabels(["fold 5", "fold 4", "fold 3", "fold 2", "fold 1"], fontsize=9.5)
ax.set_xlim(-0.7, len(COLS) - 0.3)
ax.set_ylim(-0.6, 4.6)
ax.grid(False)
ax.set_title("columns kept by the lasso, alpha = 0.1, fitted on each fold block", loc="left")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

On the early blocks the lasso keeps `XOM_vol` and `DIS_vol`; on the later ones,
`vol_5d` and `AAPL_vol`. Among near-copies it keeps one, and which one depends
on the rows.

::: {.keypoint}
A zero means the column was not needed **given the others**, on these rows. It
does not mean the column carries no information.
:::


# Ridge or lasso

<div class="compare">
<div class="compare-col">
<h3>Ridge</h3>
<p>Every column stays in with a small coefficient. Suits a table where many columns each carry a little and are correlated: the weight is spread across near-copies instead of landing on one.</p>
</div>
<div class="compare-col cmp-alt">
<h3>Lasso</h3>
<p>A short list of columns and zeros elsewhere. Suits a table where a few columns matter, or where a compact forecast is wanted. Among near-copies it keeps one, chosen by the rows.</p>
</div>
</div>

::: {.keypoint}
Cross-validate both and compare. Here ridge is slightly ahead, and the two are
within the fold spread of each other.
:::


# Elastic net

::: {.formula}
$$
\text{RSS} + \alpha\left[\, \rho \sum_{j} |\beta_j| + \tfrac{1 - \rho}{2} \sum_{j} \beta_j^2 \right]
$$
:::

The elastic net uses both penalties at once. `alpha` sets the total and
`l1_ratio`, the $\rho$ above, sets the mix: 1 is the lasso, 0 is ridge. It is
used when the columns are correlated and a compact model is still wanted.


# Searching two settings at once

```{pyodide}
from sklearn.linear_model import ElasticNet

enet = Pipeline([("scale", StandardScaler()), ("enet", ElasticNet())])
enet_grid = {"enet__alpha": [0.01, 0.1, 1], "enet__l1_ratio": [0.1, 0.5, 0.9]}

enet_search = GridSearchCV(enet, enet_grid, cv=folds, scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error")
enet_search.fit(train[columns], train["vol_next"])
print(enet_search.best_params_, -enet_search.best_score_)
```

Two keys in the grid give three times three combinations, and five folds make
forty-five fits. The best mix keeps seven columns.


# 6 · Reading the arguments {.divider}

::: {.divider-kicker}
Part 6
:::

::: {.divider-note}
Which settings matter, which do not, and how to find out.
:::


# Every setting has a default

```{pyodide}
Ridge().get_params()
```

`get_params()` lists every argument of an object and its current value.
`Ridge(alpha=1000)` changes one and leaves the rest. `help(Ridge)` prints the
documentation for all of them.


# When to change what

::: {.why-grid}
::: {.why-point}
**Always** <span>`alpha`, the penalty's strength: by cross-validation on a grid in factors of ten. `cv`: `TimeSeriesSplit` for any time series. `scoring`: the error you will report.</span>
:::
::: {.why-point}
**Sometimes** <span>`max_iter`, the passes the lasso solver may take: raise it when the warning appears. `l1_ratio`, the mix: for the elastic net. `n_jobs=-1`, folds in parallel: on your own machine.</span>
:::
::: {.why-point}
**Rarely** <span>`fit_intercept`, an unpenalised intercept: leave it on. `positive`, coefficients of zero or above: when the sign is known. `tol`, when the solver counts as finished: leave it.</span>
:::
::: {.why-point}
**Why only lasso has `max_iter`** <span>`Ridge` has a closed-form solution. `Lasso` and `ElasticNet` are solved by repeated passes over the columns, and the passes can run out.</span>
:::
:::


# The convergence warning

```
ConvergenceWarning: Objective did not converge. You might want to increase
the number of iterations, check the scale of the features or consider
increasing regularisation.
```

The lasso solver ran out of passes before settling. The result is returned
anyway, and it is slightly wrong.

::: {.why-grid}
::: {.why-point}
**Standardise first** <span>columns on wildly different scales are the usual cause, and the pipeline already handles it</span>
:::
::: {.why-point}
**Raise `max_iter`** <span>`Lasso(alpha=0.001, max_iter=10000)`. A very small alpha needs more passes than the default 1,000</span>
:::
:::


# 7 · What the coefficients mean now {.divider}

::: {.divider-kicker}
Part 7
:::

::: {.divider-note}
Penalised coefficients are for forecasting, and what that rules out.
:::


# Prediction, not inference

<div class="compare">
<div class="compare-col">
<h3>Ordinary least squares</h3>
<p>Unbiased coefficients with standard errors, so a t-test can ask whether a column has an effect. The econometrics toolkit applies.</p>
</div>
<div class="compare-col cmp-alt">
<h3>Ridge and lasso</h3>
<p>Coefficients shrunk towards zero on purpose. They are biased, they have no standard errors, and there is no <code>summary()</code>. They answer one question: what forecast.</p>
</div>
</div>

::: {.keypoint}
To test whether a column matters, fit OLS on a few columns chosen for a reason
and read the standard errors. To forecast, penalise.
:::


# What can still be said

A standardised ridge coefficient of 0.079 on `vol_5d` means: **one standard
deviation more volatility over the last five days raises the forecast by 0.079
percentage points**, with the other eighteen columns held where they are.

::: {.muted .small}
Among near-copies the split is arbitrary: 0.079 on `vol_5d` and 0.061 on
`vol_10d` could as well be the other way round. Read related columns together.
:::


# Six forecasts of the same thing

<div class="statband">
<div class="stat"><span class="stat-big">0.291</span><div class="stat-label">guess the average</div></div>
<div class="stat"><span class="stat-big">0.260</span><div class="stat-label">repeat this month</div></div>
<div class="stat"><span class="stat-big">0.237</span><div class="stat-label">one column</div></div>
<div class="stat stat-warn"><span class="stat-big">0.248</span><div class="stat-label">nineteen columns, OLS</div></div>
<div class="stat"><span class="stat-big">0.218</span><div class="stat-label">nineteen columns, ridge</div></div>
<div class="stat"><span class="stat-big">0.217</span><div class="stat-label">nineteen columns, lasso</div></div>
</div>

All six are test RMSEs in percentage points. Nineteen columns were worse than
one until the coefficients were held small; then they were the first to beat
it, with alpha chosen without the test rows.

# What stays with you {.smaller}

::: {.recap-grid}
::: {.recap-item}
**Many columns overfit**
Nineteen columns fitted the training rows better than one and forecast worse. Near-copies get large, opposite coefficients that are noise.
:::
::: {.recap-item}
**A penalty holds coefficients small**
Ridge adds $\alpha \sum \beta_j^2$, lasso adds $\alpha \sum |\beta_j|$. `Ridge(alpha=...)` fits and predicts like `LinearRegression`.
:::
::: {.recap-item}
**The penalty needs standardised columns**
It charges by coefficient size, and size depends on units. `StandardScaler` fitted on the training rows, then a `Pipeline`.
:::
::: {.recap-item}
**Alpha is a hyperparameter**
Set before `.fit()`, never changed by it. Chosen by cross-validation on the training rows, on a grid in factors of ten.
:::
::: {.recap-item}
**`GridSearchCV` runs the whole search**
Every value times every fold, the best mean kept, refitted on all training rows. `best_params_`, `best_score_`, `cv_results_`, `.predict()`.
:::
::: {.recap-item}
**Lasso gives exact zeros**
A compact model, and the kept set changes with the rows. Ridge spreads weight across correlated columns.
:::
::: {.recap-item}
**The scales are not the same**
Ridge's useful alpha was in the thousands, lasso's near 0.1. Read the validation curve rather than reusing a grid.
:::
::: {.recap-item}
**Forecasting, not inference**
Penalised coefficients are biased on purpose and have no standard errors. Fit OLS on a few chosen columns to test an effect.
:::
:::
